eklem-tipleri.summary: Joints are divided by the tissue joining the bones into fibrous, cartilaginous and synovial joints. Synovial joints are the most mobile and are subdivided by the shape of their articular surfaces.
facts: Sutures (skull), syndesmoses (e.g. tibiofibular syndesmosis), gomphoses (tooth–socket)
Synchondroses (hyaline cartilage; e.g. growth plate, 1st rib–sternum) and symphyses (fibrocartilage; e.g. pubic symphysis, intervertebral discs)
Have a joint cavity, articular cartilage, capsule, synovial membrane and synovial fluid
Plane, hinge (ginglymus – elbow), pivot (trochoid – proximal radioulnar), saddle (sellar – thumb CMC), ellipsoid (wrist), ball-and-socket (spheroidal – shoulder, hip), bicondylar (knee)
sections: Uniaxial joints (hinge, pivot) move in one plane, biaxial joints (saddle, ellipsoid) in two planes and multiaxial joints (ball-and-socket) in all planes.
The nerves that supply the muscles crossing a joint also supply the joint and the skin over it.
clinical: Osteoarthritis is degeneration of the articular cartilage; rheumatoid arthritis is autoimmune inflammation of the synovial membrane.
tus: Fibrous joints: suture, syndesmosis, gomphosis; cartilaginous joints: synchondrosis (hyaline), symphysis (fibrocartilage); the rest are synovial.
Types of synovial joint: plane, hinge, pivot, ellipsoid (condylar), saddle, ball-and-socket; bicondylar joints (knee, TMJ) are counted separately.

art-temporomandibularis.summary: The synovial joint between the condylar process of the mandible and the mandibular fossa and articular tubercle of the temporal bone. A fibrocartilaginous disc divides it into upper and lower compartments.
facts: Synovial; modified hinge (ginglymoarthrodial) joint
Head of the mandible – mandibular fossa and articular tubercle (temporal bone)
Fibrocartilage; gliding (translation) in the upper compartment, hinge movement (rotation) in the lower
Lateral (temporomandibular) ligament, sphenomandibular ligament, stylomandibular ligament
Auriculotemporal and masseteric nerves (V3)
Opening and closing, protrusion and retrusion, side-to-side (grinding) movements
clinical: When the mouth opens too wide (yawning) the head of the mandible can slip in front of the articular tubercle and the mouth cannot close (TMJ dislocation).
TMJ disorders (disc displacement, clicking, pain) are associated with tooth grinding and stress.
tus: The TMJ is a hinge-and-glide (ginglymoarthrodial) joint; its articular surfaces are fibrocartilage.
The lateral (temporomandibular) ligament is the only true reinforcement of the capsule; the sphenomandibular and stylomandibular ligaments are accessory.

discus-intervertebralis.summary: Fibrocartilaginous cushions between adjacent vertebral bodies, with a ring-shaped annulus fibrosus outside and a jelly-like nucleus pulposus in the centre. They make up about a quarter of the length of the spine.
facts: Symphysis (secondary cartilaginous joint)
Annulus fibrosus (concentric collagen lamellae), nucleus pulposus (notochord remnant, 80% water)
23 discs; none between C1 and C2 or in the sacrum and coccyx
Largely avascular in adults; nourished by diffusion from the end plates
sections: With age the nucleus pulposus loses water and the discs lose height; this underlies loss of stature and degenerative disc disease.
clinical: In disc herniation the nucleus pulposus usually tears through the annulus posterolaterally and presses on a nerve root; in the lumbar spine the L4–L5 disc affects the L5 root and the L5–S1 disc the S1 root.
In the neck the C5–C6 disc compresses the C6 root.
tus: The discs make up about 1/4 of the length of the spine; there is no disc between atlas and axis.
A cervical disc herniation compresses the root of the same number (C5–C6 → C6), a lumbar one the root below (L4–L5 → L5).

ligg-columnae.summary: Ligaments that bind the vertebrae together and stabilise the spine. Long ligaments run the whole length of the spine, short ones between neighbouring vertebrae.
facts: Anterior longitudinal ligament (front of the bodies – limits hyperextension), posterior longitudinal ligament (back of the bodies, inside the vertebral canal – limits hyperflexion), supraspinous ligament, ligamentum nuchae (in the neck)
Ligamenta flava (between the laminae, yellow elastic ligament), interspinous ligaments, intertransverse ligaments
A triangular ligament from C7 to the external occipital protuberance; gives attachment to trapezius and splenius
clinical: In lumbar puncture the needle passes through skin, supraspinous ligament, interspinous ligament, ligamentum flavum, epidural space and dura–arachnoid; a loss of resistance is felt after the ligamentum flavum.
In ankylosing spondylitis the ligaments ossify, giving a 'bamboo spine'.
tus: The anterior longitudinal ligament limits hyperextension, the posterior one hyperflexion.
The ligamentum nuchae is the triangular continuation of the supraspinous ligament in the neck; it gives attachment to trapezius and splenius.

artt-thoracis.summary: The joints of the ribs with the vertebrae (costovertebral) and with the sternum (sternocostal). They let the thoracic cage expand during breathing.
facts: Joint of the head of the rib (rib head – two neighbouring vertebral bodies) and costotransverse joint (rib tubercle – transverse process)
1st rib: synchondrosis; ribs 2–7: synovial plane joints
Interchondral joints (between cartilages 6–9), costochondral joints (rib–cartilage; hyaline cartilage union)
tus: The upper ribs move like a pump handle (anteroposterior diameter), the lower ribs like a bucket handle (transverse diameter).
Ribs 11 and 12 have no costotransverse joint.

art-sternoclavicularis.summary: The joint between the medial end of the clavicle and the manubrium and 1st costal cartilage. It is the only true joint between the upper limb and the trunk.
facts: Synovial saddle joint (functionally ball-and-socket); contains an articular disc
Anterior and posterior sternoclavicular ligaments, interclavicular ligament, costoclavicular ligament (the strongest)
Elevation–depression, protraction–retraction and rotation of the clavicle
clinical: Posterior dislocation is rare but an emergency, because it can compress the great vessels and trachea behind it.
tus: The articular disc stops the clavicle sliding medially; its strongest ligament is the costoclavicular ligament.
Posterior dislocation is rare but an emergency because it can compress the trachea and great vessels.

art-acromioclavicularis.summary: A small plane joint between the lateral end of the clavicle and the acromion of the scapula. Its main stability comes from the coracoclavicular ligament outside the joint.
facts: Synovial plane joint
Acromioclavicular ligament; coracoclavicular ligament (trapezoid and conoid ligaments) – the main stabiliser
Gliding and rotation of the scapula on the clavicle
clinical: A fall on the shoulder can separate the AC joint (unlike a shoulder dislocation); if the coracoclavicular ligament also tears, the end of the clavicle rises markedly (piano-key sign).
tus: A synovial plane joint; it lets the scapula rotate on the clavicle.
In Rockwood type III and higher injuries the coracoclavicular ligament is also torn.

art-humeri.summary: The ball-and-socket joint between the head of the humerus and the glenoid cavity of the scapula. It is the most mobile and most frequently dislocated joint in the body; its stability depends largely on the rotator cuff muscles.
facts: Synovial ball-and-socket (spheroidal) – multiaxial
Head of humerus – glenoid cavity (deepened by the glenoid labrum); only 1/3 of the head contacts the socket
Glenohumeral ligaments (superior, middle, inferior), coracohumeral ligament, transverse humeral ligament, coracoacromial ligament (roof of the joint)
Rotator cuff (SITS: supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor, subscapularis), long head of biceps tendon, labrum
Flexion–extension, abduction–adduction, internal and external rotation, circumduction
Axillary nerve, suprascapular nerve, lateral pectoral nerve
sections: The capsule is lax and weakest below (axillary recess); the long head of biceps tendon runs inside the capsule.
clinical: 95% of shoulder dislocations are anterior-inferior; the axillary nerve can be injured. Recurrent dislocations cause a tear of the anterior-inferior labrum (Bankart lesion) and a dent in the posterolateral humeral head (Hill–Sachs lesion).
In frozen shoulder (adhesive capsulitis) the capsule thickens and contracts, limiting movement in all directions.
SLAP lesion: tear of the superior labrum at the attachment of the biceps tendon.
tus: The stability of the glenohumeral joint depends more on the rotator cuff muscles than on bone.
Anterior dislocation causes a Hill–Sachs lesion (notch in the posterosuperior humeral head) and a Bankart lesion (anterior-inferior labral tear).

art-cubiti.summary: A compound joint between the humerus, ulna and radius inside a single capsule, made up of the humeroulnar, humeroradial and proximal radioulnar joints.
facts: Compound synovial joint: humeroulnar (hinge), humeroradial (ball-and-socket), proximal radioulnar (pivot)
Ulnar collateral ligament (medial), radial collateral ligament (lateral), annular ligament (ring around the radial head)
Flexion–extension (0–145°); pronation–supination at the proximal radioulnar joint
A 10–15° outward angle between arm and forearm in extension (greater in women)
sections: In the triangular hollow in front of the elbow lie, from lateral to medial, the biceps tendon, brachial artery and median nerve. The superficial median cubital vein is used for blood sampling.
clinical: Elbow dislocation is usually posterior.
Lateral epicondylitis (tennis elbow) and medial epicondylitis (golfer's elbow) are overuse injuries of the tendon origins.
In children the radial head can slip out of the annular ligament ('pulled elbow').
tus: Elbow dislocations are usually posterolateral; disruption of the triangle (olecranon and epicondyles) distinguishes dislocation from fracture.
In extension the olecranon and epicondyles lie in a straight line; in flexion they form a triangle (Hueter's triangle).

artt-radioulnares.summary: The two synovial joints between the upper and lower ends of the radius and ulna, together with the interosseous membrane between their shafts. Together they produce pronation and supination of the forearm.
facts: Pivot joint; the radial head turns in the radial notch of the ulna within the annular ligament
Pivot joint; head of ulna – ulnar notch of the radius; reinforced by the articular disc (part of the TFCC)
Its fibres run downwards and medially from radius to ulna; they transfer force from the hand and radius to the ulna
Pronation (pronator teres, pronator quadratus) and supination (supinator, biceps brachii); about 150° in total
clinical: Tears of the triangular fibrocartilage complex (TFCC) are a common cause of ulnar-sided wrist pain.
tus: At the proximal radioulnar joint the radial head turns within the annular ligament; distally the radius turns around the ulnar head.
The fibres of the interosseous membrane run down and medially from radius to ulna and transfer load from the hand to the ulna.

art-radiocarpalis.summary: The ellipsoid joint between the lower end of the radius and the articular disc and the proximal row of carpal bones (scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum). The ulna does not take part directly.
facts: Synovial ellipsoid joint (biaxial)
Carpal articular surface of the radius and articular disc – scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum
Palmar and dorsal radiocarpal ligaments, palmar ulnocarpal ligament, radial and ulnar collateral ligaments of the wrist
Flexion–extension, radial–ulnar deviation, circumduction; the midcarpal joint adds a large share of the movement
clinical: Scapholunate ligament tear is the commonest cause of wrist instability (Terry Thomas sign: a gap between scaphoid and lunate).
A wrist ganglion is a cystic swelling arising from the joint capsule.
tus: The radiocarpal joint is ellipsoid; flexion–extension and radial–ulnar deviation occur.
Ulnar deviation has a wider range than radial deviation because the radial styloid reaches further down.

artt-manus.summary: The joints between the carpal bones and metacarpals (carpometacarpal), the metacarpals and fingers (metacarpophalangeal) and between the phalanges (interphalangeal).
facts: Saddle joint at the thumb (opposition); 2nd–3rd CMC almost immobile, 4th–5th slightly mobile
Condylar joints; flexion–extension and abduction–adduction; palmar plate and collateral ligaments
Hinge joints; flexion–extension only
Collateral ligaments, palmar ligaments (volar plate), deep transverse metacarpal ligaments
clinical: Skier's thumb: tear of the ulnar collateral ligament of the thumb MCP joint.
In rheumatoid arthritis, ulnar deviation at the MCP joints, swan-neck and boutonnière deformities develop.
tus: The 1st CMC joint is a saddle joint and allows opposition; the 2nd–5th CMC joints are plane joints.
The collateral ligaments of the MCP joints are taut in flexion, so the hand is splinted with the MCP joints flexed.
